reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Caused by mutations in ALPL encoding tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase, with severe forms inherited recessively and milder forms sometimes dominant

The biochemical hallmark is a persistently low serum alkaline phosphatase with raised natural substrates, namely inorganic pyrophosphate, pyridoxal-5-phosphate (vitamin B6) and urinary phosphoethanolamine
A low alkaline phosphatase is the diagnostic clue and is the opposite of most other rickets and metabolic bone diseases, so it must not be dismissed as unimportant
Clinical severity spans a wide spectrum from lethal perinatal disease with almost unmineralised bone to mild adult disease with fractures and early tooth loss
Premature loss of the primary teeth with the root intact (before age five) is a characteristic and often early feature
Infantile forms can cause hypercalcaemia, vitamin B6-dependent seizures, nephrocalcinosis and craniosynostosis
Enzyme replacement therapy (asfotase alfa) has transformed outcomes for severe paediatric disease
Bisphosphonates and other antiresorptives are generally avoided because they are pyrophosphate analogues and may worsen the condition
reference.pathophysiology: Hypophosphatasia results from deficient activity of tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase, an enzyme that normally hydrolyses inorganic pyrophosphate at the mineralising surface of bone and teeth. Because inorganic pyrophosphate is a potent inhibitor of hydroxyapatite crystal formation, its accumulation blocks normal mineralisation, producing rickets and osteomalacia despite adequate calcium and phosphate. Accumulation of pyridoxal-5-phosphate impairs vitamin B6 delivery to the brain and can cause seizures in severe forms, while phosphoethanolamine accumulates and is excreted in the urine.
additionalDifferentials: Achondrogenesis and other lethal perinatal skeletal dysplasias
additionalInvestigations: Serum alkaline phosphatase, interpreted against age-appropriate reference ranges (characteristically low)
Serum and urinary substrate measurement (pyridoxal-5-phosphate, inorganic pyrophosphate, urinary phosphoethanolamine)
Molecular testing of ALPL to confirm the diagnosis and guide counselling
Skeletal radiographs to demonstrate rickets, poor mineralisation and metaphyseal tongues of lucency
Serum calcium and renal imaging to detect hypercalcaemia and nephrocalcinosis
Dental assessment documenting premature loss of primary teeth
redFlags: Perinatal or infantile respiratory failure from an unmineralised, poorly compliant chest
Vitamin B6-responsive seizures in an infant with a low alkaline phosphatase
Symptomatic hypercalcaemia with nephrocalcinosis and renal impairment
Craniosynostosis with raised intracranial pressure in infantile disease
reference.prognosis: The perinatal and infantile forms were historically often lethal, but enzyme replacement therapy has markedly improved survival and skeletal outcome; milder childhood and adult forms have a good prognosis with attention to fractures, dental health and pain.
pitfalls: Ignoring a low alkaline phosphatase as a laboratory artefact rather than a diagnostic clue
Giving bisphosphonates, which can aggravate the mineralisation defect
Supplementing with high-dose vitamin D reflexively, risking worsening hypercalcaemia
Misclassifying severe perinatal disease as osteogenesis imperfecta
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Give enzyme replacement therapy with asfotase alfa for paediatric-onset disease, particularly the perinatal and infantile forms, to improve skeletal mineralisation and survival
Treat vitamin B6-dependent seizures in infantile disease with pyridoxine
Avoid bisphosphonates and other antiresorptives, which are pyrophosphate analogues that can worsen the disease, and avoid excessive calcium and vitamin D supplementation
Manage fractures and poor healing with orthopaedic input and provide analgesia for bone pain
Provide specialist dental care for premature loss of the primary teeth
Monitor for hypercalcaemia, nephrocalcinosis and craniosynostosis in the infantile forms
Refer to metabolic and skeletal dysplasia services and offer genetic counselling with ALPL-based family testing given recessive and dominant inheritance
